speaker_role: journalist/researcher and author (Jeff Selingo, higher-ed journalist), interviewed by the Grown and Flown host; not a former admissions officer himself
commercial_incentive: Heavily promotes his forthcoming book 'Dream School,' including a pre-order bonus guide and exclusive webinars tied to proof of purchase.
key_insights: Cites his own survey of 3,000+ parents: only 16% said prestige personally mattered to them, but 61% believed prestige mattered to other parents in their community -- suggesting perceived social pressure inflates prestige obsession beyond people's actual stated values.

Argues an elite/Ivy-type degree gives a modest statistical edge ('two lottery tickets instead of one') rather than a guaranteed outcome, citing a Fortune 500 CEO study spanning roughly 300 different colleges where some non-elite schools produced more CEOs than some elite ones.

Describes 'big fish, small pond' research showing students, particularly in STEM, are more likely to persist in a challenging major at a less competitive school than at a highly selective one, partly due to stronger faculty/TA support versus a sink-or-swim culture.

Explains 'yield management': as students apply to more schools (partly fueled by test-optional policies), colleges defer or reject strong applicants they doubt will enroll in order to protect their yield rate and prestige metrics, independent of qualification.

Notes that headline 'more selective than ever' statistics mostly reflect more applications per student, not fewer admitted or enrolled students, since most selective schools' class sizes have stayed roughly flat for decades.

Recommends researching a school's career center and department-level (not just overall) outcomes -- e.g., tracing alumni via LinkedIn or using the government's College Scorecard -- since hiring tends to be regional and major-specific.

His 75-school 'dream school' list was built from objective filters (1,000+ students, roughly 30%+ acceptance rate) plus NSSE engagement data, earnings/ROI data, and other outcomes research, aiming for 'accessible and excellent' schools rather than another prestige ranking.
specific_numbers_or_facts: Speaker says his survey of 3,000+ parents found 16% valued prestige personally vs 61% believing other parents valued it.
Speaker says Duke's yield is around 60% versus a roughly 40% typical yield industry-wide 20 years ago, while many less selective schools now yield only 10-20%.
Speaker cites Clemson's out-of-state yield as about 15%, explaining why strong out-of-state early-action applicants sometimes get deferred there.
Speaker says a data-analytics certificate (e.g., Alteryx) paired with a marketing major could raise starting salary by roughly $15,000-$25,000.
Speaker says the high school Class of 2025 is the largest graduating class for at least the next 15 years, after which application volume may decline somewhat.
notable_or_distinctive: Reframes 'increased selectivity' as largely a statistical artifact of rising applications per student rather than genuinely fewer spots, and grounds prestige-vs-outcomes claims in named third-party datasets (Lightcast, NSSE, College Scorecard, Bain, Burning Glass).
reliability_notes: Data points are attributed to named sources (Lightcast, NSSE, Bain & Company, College Scorecard) but recalled verbally in an interview without on-screen citations, and the segment doubles as marketing for his book and paid webinars.
